name: EcoFlow Delta Pro
summary: The right outage power for apartments, condos, medical devices and anyone who cannot run an engine safely.
verdict: The Delta Pro is a big lithium iron phosphate battery with an inverter, not a generator in the combustion sense, and that is precisely why it is here. With no engine, it can sit in a kitchen or bedroom running a refrigerator, a CPAP, a modem and lights with no carbon monoxide risk and no noise. EcoFlow rates the base unit at 3.6kWh of storage and 3,600 watts of continuous output, and extra battery packs expand the system. It recharges from a wall outlet, solar panels, a vehicle or EcoFlow's own smart gas generator, which turns it into a quiet buffer for a fuel-burning unit. The constraint is arithmetic: a typical refrigerator uses 1 to 2kWh a day, so one Delta Pro carries essentials for one to three days without solar. Expect roughly $2,500 to $3,500 at the time of writing, depending on bundles.

name: EcoFlow DELTA 2 Battery Station
summary: The small choice for apartments, CPAP users and brief outages, or as the quiet half of a gas-inverter setup.
verdict: A battery station earns a place here because plenty of people shopping for a small generator really want small, quiet power, and a battery is the only option that can sit inside the house. EcoFlow rates the DELTA 2 at 1,024 watt-hours of LiFePO4 storage and 1,800 watts of output, enough to start and run a modern refrigerator for most of a day or a CPAP for several nights. It makes no noise, needs no fuel or oil, and recharges from a wall outlet in about an hour, from solar panels, or from a small gas inverter running outdoors. name: Anker SOLIX F3800 Portable Power Station
summary: The battery to buy when you want silent, fuel-free backup that can genuinely start a 240V well pump.
verdict: A well pump uses surprisingly little energy; the hard part is the starting surge and the 240 volts. Anker's SOLIX F3800 addresses both, which is why it leads the battery options here. Anker rates it at 3,840 watt-hours of LFP and 6,000 watts of output with 120/240V split-phase capability, so it can feed a double-pole pump circuit through a compatible transfer switch or Anker's home backup hardware, installed by an electrician. By the runtime math in this guide, a typical household's daily pumping uses well under 1kWh, so the pump barely dents the battery; it is the refrigerator, freezer and everything else that sets how long it lasts. Expansion batteries and solar input stretch an outage into days. Check its published surge rating against your pump maker's sizing table before relying on it for a 1.5 HP motor. name: Goal Zero Yeti 1500X Lithium Power Station
summary: Worth it for off-grid and rugged use when it is discounted; otherwise LiFePO4 rivals give more for the money.
verdict: Goal Zero has made portable power for longer than most brands on this list, and the Yeti 1500X shows it in its build quality and accessory range. It is rated at 1,516 watt-hours with 2,000 watts of continuous output, and its built-in charge controller handles strong solar input. The battery is lithium NMC rather than LiFePO4, which saves weight for the capacity but brings a shorter rated cycle life, roughly in the hundreds of full cycles rather than the thousands. For a cabin, an overlanding rig or a home kit that sees occasional deep cycles, that is acceptable; for daily cycling, an LFP unit will last longer. The strongest case for it is toughness plus the panel, link and home-integration accessories. At full list price it is expensive per watt-hour, so wait for a sale. Expect roughly $1,300 to $2,000 at the time of writing, depending on bundles and discounts.

name: Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 Portable Power Station
summary: The best no-installation backup for overnight outages with a fridge and medical device.
verdict: Many households do not need a panel-connected system at all. If your outages are typically a stormy night rather than a week, and your critical loads all plug into ordinary outlets, a 2kWh unit you can carry from the kitchen to the bedroom is the most practical backup there is. Jackery lists the Explorer 2000 v2 at 2,042Wh and 2,200W. By the runtime rule, that capacity supplies a fridge, router, CPAP and lights averaging about 105W for roughly 16 hours, a full night and most of the next day, and the inverter has enough headroom for a fridge start-up with everything else running, or a quick microwave meal. The limits are clear and worth respecting: it is 120V only, it cannot be expanded, and anything hardwired, such as a furnace blower or many sump pumps, still needs a proper inlet and transfer switch to reach it. If you suspect you will want 240V or more storage later, the Delta Pro 3 or F3800 is the better long-term buy. If not, this is the sweet spot of simplicity and runtime.

Because a newer 2kWh model, the Delta 3 Max, now sits above it in EcoFlow's range, the Delta 2 Max is regularly discounted. When it is, it is one of the cheapest ways to get 2kWh of LFP and real expansion in a single EcoFlow box.

name: EcoFlow Delta Pro Ultra Home Backup Power Station
summary: A home battery system sold through power-station channels; worth it only if you are wiring it into the house permanently.
verdict: The Delta Pro Ultra is technically sold alongside EcoFlow's power stations, but it behaves like a home battery. It is a modular system: an inverter unit that EcoFlow rates at 7,200W with 120/240V output, sitting on top of one or more 6kWh LFP battery modules. Stack more batteries for more storage, or link inverters for more output, and the system scales well past anything else EcoFlow sells. Paired with the Smart Home Panel 2, it can switch over the house automatically when the grid drops and manage which circuits stay on. Its solar input is sized for a permanent array rather than folding panels. None of that comes cheap, and none of it is portable: each module is a heavy lift, and the whole system is meant to live in a garage or utility room on a dedicated install. If you are pricing this, also price a permanent wall-mounted home battery and a standby generator before you decide.

name: Jackery Explorer 300 Plus Portable Power Station
summary: A good small station for devices and CPAP nights; do not buy it expecting to run kitchen appliances.
verdict: The Explorer 300 Plus is Jackery's small LFP station and its most direct answer to EcoFlow's River 3 series. Jackery lists it at 288Wh of storage and 300W of output in a case of about 8 pounds, small enough to toss in a daypack or behind a car seat. name: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 Portable Power Station
summary: Buy it over the original C1000 when the price gap is small; the extra output and faster charging are real upgrades.
verdict: The C1000 Gen 2 is a ground-up redesign rather than a cosmetic refresh. Anker rates it at 1,024 watt-hours of LFP storage, a little less than the original, but raises continuous output to 2,000 watts, which gives more margin for kitchen appliances, power tools and refrigerator start-up surges. If the two are within a small price band, the Gen 2 is the better buy; if the original is on a deep discount, it still does the job very well.

name: Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus Portable Power Station
summary: Choose it over the F3800 only if you plan a large solar array; otherwise the original is the better value.
verdict: The F3800 Plus keeps everything that makes the F3800 the best Anker for home backup, including 3,840 watt-hours of LFP storage and 6,000 watts of 120/240V output by Anker's rating, and focuses the upgrade on charging. Anker's spec sheet lists a higher solar input ceiling than the original, which matters if you plan a large fixed or ground-mounted array: more panels can feed the battery at once, so it refills faster in the hours of strong sun you actually get during a multi-day outage. If you plan to run a couple of portable panels, or mostly recharge from the grid between outages, the extra headroom does nothing for you and the original F3800 is the better value. If you are building a serious solar-plus-battery setup that should carry the house through several days, the Plus is the one to buy.
